title: Walking Route Planner: Pedestrian Routes and GPX
description: Plan a pedestrian route between two places with the Walking Route Planner — distance, time estimate and GPX export. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a cross-town walk routed on footpaths usually measures a little longer than the same line by car — and unlike the car's version, every yard of it is legal to walk.
quick_answer: The Walking Route Planner finds a route between places on the pedestrian network — streets and paths people on foot can use — and reports its distance with a walking-time estimate. Set start and destination, review the line, and export GPX if the walk should live on a device.
steps_intro: Walkers need their own network. Plan on it, not on the car's:

Visitors on foot see the city properly. A planned pedestrian route turns wandering into a tour with a known end.

faq: Is the route accessibility-aware?
It routes on the pedestrian network the data describes. Step-free guarantees need surface and step data that is recorded unevenly — treat the route as a plan to check, not a promise of access.
Does it use live closures?
No. Footpath closures and works are local and fleeting; the route reflects the mapped network, and your eyes handle the day's diversions.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Walkers route around traffic by existing; the estimate is time on feet, not time in queues.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Paths wind and detour around what feet cannot cross. The planner's figure is the walkable distance — the honest one.
Can route results change over time?
Yes — new paths, new bridges, corrected data. Re-plan a standing walk each season.
Can I export the route?
Yes, GPX — for phones, watches and the other planners that import it.
Running the same route?
The Running Route Planner is the same network tuned for runs, with its own export habits.
Can it route through a park after dark?
Paths are data; opening hours are policy. The plan shows the way that exists; gates decide whether it is open.
The route uses a road with no pavement.
Pedestrian data sometimes includes such links where no alternative is mapped. Judge the segment as you would on foot — the plan is advice, not armour.
Multiple stops on foot?
Plan leg by leg; each becomes its own route, and the day chains them as surely as the multi-stop drivers do.
